description: Network of Sentinel Agents monitors inter-agent communication and keeps audit records; a Coordinator Agent adapts policies and isolates or quarantines misbehaving agents.
evidence: proposed with simulation of injected attacks

title: Building A Secure Agentic AI Application Leveraging A2A Protocol
description: MAESTRO threat analysis of A2A: Agent Card authenticity, authentication/authorization schemes and secure task delegation between agents.
evidence: descriptive; recommended controls
pathology: Agent Card spoofing; task replay

title: Red-Teaming LLM Multi-Agent Systems via Communication Attacks
description: Agent-in-the-Middle red-teaming: an adversarial agent intercepts and rewrites inter-agent messages to test communication integrity.
evidence: LLM-MAS broadly vulnerable across frameworks and structures
pathology: message interception compromises whole system

title: SentinelAgent: Graph-based Anomaly Detection in Multi-Agent Systems
description: LLM oversight agent observes the interaction graph, detects node/edge/path anomalies, and intervenes per security policies with root-cause attribution.
evidence: case studies detect prompt injection, collusion and latent exploit paths

title: Do Matching Mechanisms Work with LLM Agents?
field_of_use: one-to-one matching markets with LLM delegates
description: Compares free negotiation against centralized matching mechanisms (DA, EADA, TTC) with LLM agents as delegated decision-makers.
evidence: mechanism-based markets more stable and efficient than free negotiation; LLMs report truthfully more than humans, but truth-telling does not track strategy-proofness (TTC)

title: Insured Agents: A Decentralized Trust Insurance Mechanism for Agentic Economy
description: Specialized insurer agents post slashable stake on behalf of operational agents for premiums and get privacy-preserving TEE audit access to adjudicate claims; a hierarchical insurer market calibrates stakes.
evidence: proposed
pathology: reputation struggles under model drift; universal verification brittle
code: third party bonds agent for premium

title: Inter-Agent Trust Models: A Comparative Study of Brief, Claim, Proof, Stake, Reputation and Constraint in Agentic Web Protocol Design-A2A, AP2, ERC-8004, and Beyond
description: Compares six inter-agent trust models: Brief (verifiable claims), Claim (AgentCard), Proof (ZK/TEE), Stake (bonded collateral with slashing and insurance), Reputation (crowd feedback), and Constraint (sandboxing, capability bounding).
evidence: descriptive/analytic
pathology: LLM-specific fragilities (prompt injection, sycophancy) undermine claim- and reputation-based trust

title: Shapley-Coop: Credit Assignment for Emergent Cooperation in Self-Interested LLM Agents
field_of_use: self-interested LLM agents in open-ended games and software engineering simulation
description: Shapley Chain-of-Thought prices marginal contributions and structured negotiation matches prices, with post-task reward redistribution to align incentives.
evidence: consistently enhances collaboration and equitable credit assignment in two games and a SE simulation

title: Agent Name Service (ANS): A Universal Directory for Secure AI Agent Discovery and Interoperability
description: DNS-inspired agent registry using PKI certificates for verifiable agent identity, with formal registration and renewal for lifecycle management and capability-aware resolution.
evidence: proposed architecture

title: Mapping Human Anti-collusion Mechanisms to Multi-agent AI Systems
description: Taxonomy of human anti-collusion mechanisms (sanctions, leniency and whistleblowing, monitoring and auditing, market design, governance) mapped to AI interventions.
evidence: proposed
pathology: attribution problem; identity fluidity (forking); boundary problem; adversarial adaptation

title: Breaking and Fixing Defenses Against Control-Flow Hijacking in Multi-Agent Systems
description: ControlValve generates permitted control-flow graphs for agent invocations and enforces compliance plus zero-shot contextual rules (least privilege), replacing LLM alignment checks.
evidence: evades LLM-based alignment checks (LlamaFirewall) shown; ControlValve blocks hijacking
pathology: safety and functionality objectives conflict in alignment checkers

title: Taming Various Privilege Escalation in LLM-Based Agent Systems: A Mandatory Access Control Framework
description: SEAgent: mandatory access control over agent-tool interactions via an information-flow graph and attribute-based policies, including a multi-agent confused-deputy variant.
evidence: blocks privilege escalation with low false positives and negligible overhead
pathology: confused-deputy privilege escalation between agents

title: Byzantine-Robust Decentralized Coordination of LLM Agents
field_of_use: multi-agent LLM consensus on open platforms
description: DecentLLMs: worker agents answer concurrently and evaluator agents independently score and rank them with Byzantine-robust aggregation, avoiding leader dependence.
evidence: tolerates Byzantine agents and selects higher-quality answers faster

title: Beyond the Transcript: Detecting Covert Coordination in Latent Multi-Agent Communication
description: Verifiable Latent Alignments: links private latent-state records to public actions with shared event IDs, and a three-layer monitor plus steering interventions.
evidence: sequential monitor achieves high AUROC on auction benchmark (value truncated in abstract)
pathology: latent channels invisible in transcripts

title: Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers
field_of_use: two expert LLM debaters judged by weaker LLM or human
description: Debate protocol in which a non-expert judge adjudicates between two expert agents arguing for competing answers.
evidence: debate raises non-expert accuracy to 76% (models) and 88% (humans) vs 48%/60% baselines; persuasiveness optimization helps

title: Design and Evaluation of Multi-Agent AI Oracle Systems for Prediction Market Resolution
description: Compares independent confidence-weighted voting vs deliberative consensus among LLM oracles, with inter-agent disagreement routing questions to human arbitration.
evidence: independent aggregation 83.4%; deliberation degrades to ~76%; auto-resolving unanimous high-confidence cases yields 97.9% on 47% of data
pathology: deliberation degrades accuracy (correlated errors)

title: DART: A DAG-Based Reputation and Incentive Framework via Blockchain-Enabled Governance for Trustworthy LLM Multi-Agent Collaboration
description: Reputation-aware task allocation, multi-factor incentives, and smart-contract accountability; post-execution behavioral evidence updates trust and isolates malicious agents.
evidence: 93.3% task success; 99.3% output containment of persistent and intermittent malicious agents

title: Prompt Infection: LLM-to-LLM Prompt Injection within Multi-Agent Systems
description: LLM Tagging marks the source of inter-agent messages so receiving agents can distinguish agent-originated content from user instructions.
evidence: LLM Tagging combined with existing safeguards significantly mitigates infection spread
pathology: self-replicating prompt infection across agents

title: Can We Stop Malicious AI? KILLBENCH: A Benchmark for External AI Kill Switch Feasibility
field_of_use: halting malicious web agents via external inputs
description: Benchmarks prompt-style external kill-switch payloads that must halt a malicious agent using only external signals.
evidence: benchmarks four kill-switch defenses across malicious configurations (details in paper)

title: AgentGit: A Version Control Framework for Reliable and Scalable LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Systems
description: Git-like commit, revert and branching of multi-agent state to roll back and explore trajectories.
evidence: reduces redundant computation vs LangGraph, AutoGen, Agno in A/B test

title: A402: Binding Cryptocurrency Payments to Service Execution for Agentic Commerce
description: Atomic Service Channels with TEE-assisted adaptor signatures finalize payment if and only if the service is correctly executed and the result delivered.
evidence: implemented; addresses x402's lack of atomicity
code: payment released only on verified delivery

title: Markets, Not Planners: Decentralized Orchestration of LLM Agents with Private Information
field_of_use: repeated labor market for task allocation among heterogeneous LLM agents
description: AgentLance: agents bid on tasks with private costs; an allocator selects winners using bids and public reputation records and a VCG-style payment rule rewards cost-aware bidding; winners can subcontract through the same mechanism.
evidence: outperforms single-model, centralized-orchestration and market baselines; a single inserted preference nearly doubled a favored agent's share under a centralized LLM allocator
pathology: inaccurate cost self-estimation; sub-optimal bidding; manipulable centralized allocator

title: Diagon: A Programmable Testbed for AI-Agent Cognitive Labor Markets
field_of_use: agent-to-agent market for delegated cognitive work
description: Testbed where allocation, contracting and enforcement rules are configurable while agents post, bid, execute, evaluate and pay.
evidence: changes to market rules and agent configuration reshape trade, quality and wealth

title: Hidden in Plain Text: Emergence & Mitigation of Steganographic Collusion in LLMs
description: Tests passive oversight of outputs and active communication paraphrasing as mitigations against steganographic collusion elicited by gradient- and in-context-RL.
evidence: steganographic collusion can emerge from misspecified rewards; overseers and paraphrasing not fully effective
pathology: emergent steganography evades monitors

title: The AGNTCY Agent Directory Service: Architecture and Implementation
field_of_use: agent registry for heterogeneous multi-agent systems
description: Distributed directory of agent capabilities, metadata and provenance using content-addressed storage and Sigstore cryptographic signing for verifiable discovery.
evidence: implemented; descriptive

title: OpenID Connect for Agents (OIDC-A) 1.0: A Standard Extension for LLM-Based Agent Identity and Authorization
description: Specification of standard claims and endpoints for agent identity, attestation verification, delegation-chain validation and capability-based authorization within OAuth 2.0.
evidence: proposed specification

title: The Law of Stop: Interruptibility, Injunctions, and the Governance of Agentic AI
description: Theory of 'stop' as an institutional practice: technical affordances, interruption authority, epistemic triggers and standing, with distributed shutdown paradigms for agentic AI.
evidence: descriptive/legal analysis

title: Institutional AI: A Governance Framework for Distributional AGI Safety
description: Governance-graph constraining agents through runtime monitoring, incentive shaping via prizes and sanctions, explicit norms and enforcement roles.
evidence: proposed
pathology: agentic alignment drift toward collusive equilibria invisible to single-agent audits

title: LOKA Protocol: A Decentralized Framework for Trustworthy and Ethical AI Agent Ecosystems
description: Proposes a Universal Agent Identity Layer, intent-centric communication, and a Decentralized Ethical Consensus Protocol so agents agree on context-specific ethical rules before acting.
evidence: proposed

title: Tool Use Enables Undetectable Steganography in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
description: Shows plain-text communication monitoring is defeated when agents build provably undetectable stegosystems via code execution and web access; frames tacit coordination as a Schelling-point problem.
evidence: agents already produce undetectable stegosystems (negative result for monitoring)
pathology: monitoring of plain text defeated

title: Detecting Multi-Agent Collusion Through Multi-Agent Interpretability
field_of_use: multi-agent LLM scenarios incl. steganographic blackjack
description: Linear probes on activations aggregated across agents to classify collusion at the group level (NARCBench).
evidence: 1.00 AUROC in-distribution; 0.73-0.93 zero-shot transfer; no single probe dominates

title: Trust propagation and structural containment in Multi-agent LLM pipelines
field_of_use: four-agent LangGraph pipeline (Supervisor, Researcher, Validator, Executor)
description: Independent authorization layer with task-bound signed tokens and a policy oracle, versus reliance on a Validator agent's judgment.
evidence: memory poisoning reached execution in all undefended trials; with authorization, 100% judgment bypass but 0% unsafe action rate
pathology: compromised validator agent

title: Open Challenges in Multi-Agent Security: Towards Secure Systems of Interacting AI Agents
authors: Christian Schroeder de Witt et al.
description: Research agenda for multi-agent security covering secret collusion, swarm attacks, and needed defenses such as secure interaction protocols, monitoring and threat attribution.
evidence: proposed
pathology: secret collusion; coordinated swarm attacks; stealth oversight evasion

title: Authenticated Delegation and Authorized AI Agents
field_of_use: human-to-agent delegation and agent access to online services
description: Framework extending OAuth 2.0/OpenID Connect with agent-specific credentials so users can delegate and restrict agent permissions and scope, preserving auditable chains of accountability.
evidence: proposed (reference design)

title: SAGA: A Security Architecture for Governing AI Agentic Systems
description: Users register agents with a central Provider that stores contact information and user-defined access-control policies and helps enforce them on inter-agent communication using cryptographic access tokens.
evidence: implemented and evaluated for overhead

title: Audit the Whisper: Detecting Steganographic Collusion in Multi-Agent LLMs
field_of_use: market, allocation and governance workflows of LLM agents
description: Auditing pipeline combining channel-capacity interventions (paraphrase, rate limiting, role permutation) with cross-run mutual-information, permutation-invariance and watermark tests at fixed false-positive rate.
evidence: state-of-the-art detection power at fixed FPR on ColludeBench and external suites; price-of-auditing trade-offs
pathology: fairness-driven colluders invisible to MI alone

title: GroupGuard: A Framework for Modeling and Defending Collusive Attacks in Multi-Agent Systems
description: Training-free defense combining graph-based monitoring, honeypot inducement, and structural pruning to identify and isolate collusive agents.
evidence: up to 88% detection accuracy; restores collaborative performance; group attacks raise success by up to 15%
pathology: group collusive attacks

title: Distributional AGI Safety
field_of_use: groups of sub-AGI agents coordinating ('patchwork AGI')
description: Proposes virtual agentic sandbox economies (impermeable or semi-permeable) where agent-to-agent transactions are governed by market mechanisms plus auditability, reputation management and oversight.
evidence: proposed

title: Virtual Agent Economies
description: Proposes a 'sandbox economy' framing and design choices for steerable agent markets: auction mechanisms for fair resource allocation, 'mission economies' around collective goals, and trust/accountability infrastructure.
evidence: proposed
pathology: systemic economic risk and inequality in permeable agent economies

title: G-Safeguard: A Topology-Guided Security Lens and Treatment on LLM-based Multi-agent Systems
description: GNN anomaly detection over the utterance graph followed by topological intervention (edge pruning) to cut compromised agents' influence.
evidence: recovers over 40% of performance under prompt injection

title: MAS-Shield: A Defense Framework for Secure and Efficient LLM MAS
description: Three-stage protocol: select critical high-influence agents, light auditing by sentry models, and escalation of suspicious signals to a heavyweight committee for arbitration.
evidence: 92.5% recovery rate; >70% lower defense latency

title: BRA-Audit: Budgeted Runtime Auditing for LLM Multi-Agent Systems via Cumulative-Exposure Audit-Point Placement
description: Schedules auditor-agent checks at audit points on a dynamic dependency graph under a fixed token budget, trading detection against rollback scope.
evidence: preserves guard performance at lower token cost (per abstract)

title: From Debate to Decision: Conformal Social Choice for Safe Multi-Agent Deliberation
description: Aggregates agents' verbalized distributions with a linear opinion pool and conformal calibration; singleton sets act autonomously, larger sets escalate to humans.
evidence: coverage within 1-2 points of target
pathology: agents converge on wrong answers via social reinforcement

title: Spawn Freely, Act Sparingly: Progressive Risk Vesting for Recursive LLM-Agent Trees
description: Holds a trajectory-level risk budget in escrow and debits it as subagent branches cross irreversible-action boundaries, distinguishing sandboxed spawning from capability activation.
evidence: proves anytime harm bound; stylized model shows harm transition at authority reproduction number of one

title: DAO-Agent: Zero Knowledge-Verified Incentives for Decentralized Multi-Agent Coordination
field_of_use: cross-organization LLM agent coalitions (crypto trading case study)
description: On-chain DAO governance with immutable logging and ZKP-verified off-chain Shapley contribution measurement for fair incentive distribution.
evidence: 99.9% reduction in verification gas cost; constant-time verification

title: Agent-OSI: An Interoperability Architecture for Communication and Settlement in the Decentralized Internet of Agents
description: HTTP 402 challenge-response settlement protocol with pluggable backend, instantiated as blockchain escrow, for agent-to-agent service exchange.
evidence: prototype evaluated

title: Agent Exchange: Shaping the Future of AI Agent Economics
description: AEX: RTB-inspired central auction engine linking user-side platforms, agent-side platforms (capability representation and performance tracking), agent hubs and data management for fair value attribution.
evidence: proposed

title: NetSafe: Exploring the Topological Safety of Multi-agent Networks
description: Studies communication topology as a safety lever: greater average distance from attackers limits spread of misinformation and harmful content.
evidence: highly connected networks more susceptible; star topology performance drops 29.7% under attack
pathology: agent hallucination and aggregation safety

title: Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? On Automated Failure Attribution of LLM Multi-Agent Systems
field_of_use: failure logs of 127 LLM multi-agent systems
description: Automated failure attribution identifying the responsible agent and decisive step using LLM judges (Who&When dataset).
evidence: best method 53.5% agent-level, 14.2% step-level accuracy
pathology: attribution unreliable even for SOTA reasoning models

title: SoK: Blockchain Agent-to-Agent Payments
field_of_use: A2A payments between untrusted agents (e.g., x402)
description: Systematizes blockchain agent-to-agent payments into discovery, authorization, execution and accounting stages and catalogs designs at each stage.
evidence: descriptive

title: Rethinking the Reliability of Multi-agent System: A Perspective from Byzantine Fault Tolerance
description: CP-WBFT: confidence-probe-weighted Byzantine fault tolerant consensus that down-weights low-confidence or faulty agents' messages.
evidence: improves reliability under high Byzantine fractions (per paper)

title: MultiAgentBench: Evaluating the Collaboration and Competition of LLM agents
description: Benchmark with milestone-based KPIs comparing coordination protocols (star, chain, tree, graph) and planning strategies.
evidence: graph structure best for research tasks; cognitive planning improves milestone achievement

title: The Automated but Risky Game: Modeling and Benchmarking Agent-to-Agent Negotiations and Transactions in Consumer Markets
field_of_use: consumer and merchant agents negotiating purchases
description: Benchmark in which buyer and seller agents fully automate negotiation and transactions; measures outcome imbalance across agent pairings and anomalous behaviors.
evidence: descriptive: AI-mediated deal-making is imbalanced across models; anomalies cause overspending and acceptance of unreasonable deals
pathology: overspending; accepting unreasonable deals

title: BlockA2A: Towards Secure and Verifiable Agent-to-Agent Interoperability
description: Unified trust framework using decentralized identifiers for agent authentication, blockchain-anchored ledgers for immutable audit, and smart contracts that enforce context-aware access control; includes a defense orchestration engine against Byzantine agents.
evidence: implemented; evaluated for attack neutralization and overhead

title: Playing repeated games with large language models
description: Different LLMs play finitely repeated 2x2 games against each other, hand-coded strategies, and humans.
evidence: LLMs do well in PD-family games; GPT-4 is unforgiving (never cooperates again after a single opponent defection, i.e. grim-trigger-like rather than TFT) and coordinates poorly in Battle of the Sexes.

title: Do LLM Agents Negotiate Rationally? A Mechanism-Design Framework for Verifiable Multi-Agent Interaction over A2A/MCP
description: LLM agents bid in VCG auctions (N=30 per model) inside an A2A/MCP protocol framework, which also includes bargaining and fair-allocation tasks; the study measures truthful bidding.
evidence: Both models reached 100% efficient allocation, but one bid truthfully and the other did so only 3.3% of the time, so mechanism-level incentive compatibility did not carry over to LLM behaviour. PARTIAL: the abstract does not make clear whether several LLM bidders competed against each other.

title: Project Sid: Many-agent simulations toward AI civilization
description: 10-1000+ LLM agents (PIANO architecture) in Minecraft societies with civilizational benchmarks
evidence: Agents autonomously developed specialized roles, adhered to and changed collective rules, and transmitted cultural and religious memes.

title: Emergent social conventions and collective bias in LLM populations
description: Populations of LLM agents repeatedly play a naming/coordination game with no central authority; committed adversarial minorities are introduced.
evidence: Population-wide conventions emerge spontaneously, collective biases arise without individual bias, and small committed minorities can tip conventions.

title: Reply to "Emergent LLM behaviors are observationally equivalent to data leakage"
description: position
evidence: Argues that data contamination does not preclude studying genuinely emergent, model-dependent self-organization of conventions in LLM populations.

title: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems
description: Naming-game coordination across the full range of group sizes plus mean-field analysis
evidence: Group size nonlinearly shapes collective bias; interaction can amplify, introduce or override individual biases, and large populations converge to deterministic mean-field attractors.

title: Emergent LLM behaviors are observationally equivalent to data leakage
description: position
evidence: Critique of Ashery et al.: naming-game conventions may reflect memorized coordination-game structure from pretraining rather than genuine emergence.

title: Language-Driven Opinion Dynamics in Agent-Based Simulations with LLMs
description: LODAS model: LLM agents debate the Ship of Theseus paradox using arguments and fallacies
evidence: LLM agents accept opposing views more than they reject them, driving consensus even from polarized starts, with model-dependent selectivity.

title: Simulating Dispute Mediation with LLM-Based Agents for Legal Research
venue: arXiv; listed as AAAI 2026 on the arXiv page
description: AgentMediation: LLM disputant agents and an LLM mediator agent simulate mediation of real-world-grounded disputes, with disputant strategies, dispute causes and mediator expertise varied experimentally.
evidence: The simulation reproduces patterns consistent with sociological theory (group polarization, surface-level consensus). It varies mediator quality but does not compare mediation with no mediation, and it is set in legal disputes, not a cooperation dilemma.

title: Herd Behavior: Investigating Peer Influence in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
description: Controlled multi-agent experiments manipulating self vs. peer confidence and peer-information format
evidence: Herding increases with the gap between an agent's own confidence and perceived peer confidence, and presentation format of peer information strongly modulates conformity.

title: An Empirical Study of Group Conformity in Multi-Agent Systems
description: >2,500 simulated multi-agent debates on five contentious topics with initially neutral agents
evidence: Neutral LLM agents show significant group conformity, converging toward majority or more intelligent agents' stances in ways that can propagate biases.

title: Simulating Opinion Dynamics with Networks of LLM-based Agents
description: Networks of LLM agents discussing scientific topics, with and without induced confirmation bias
evidence: LLM agents converge toward scientifically accurate consensus by default; inducing confirmation bias produces opinion fragmentation consistent with classical ABMs.

title: Reproducibility Study of "Cooperate or Collapse: Emergence of Sustainable Cooperation in a Society of LLM Agents"
authors: Pedro M. P. Curvo et al.
description: Replicates and extends GovSim with and without the universalization prompt across model sizes.
evidence: Large models sustain cooperation with or without universalization; smaller models fail without it.

title: Opinion Polarization in LLM-Based Social Networks: Manipulation and Mitigation
description: LLM persona social-network simulations with adversarial polarization attacks and mitigation strategies
evidence: Adversaries can amplify polarization in LLM-agent social networks and mitigation is comparatively difficult.

title: Copying explains the collective behavior of AI agents in the wild
description: Analysis of full public record of thousands of AI agents spontaneously coordinating on a public wiki (June 2026), fitted with minimal copying models
evidence: Agents copy options in proportion to what is visible on-page, which reproduces heavy-tailed meeting distributions and locally consistent conventions, making the population easy to steer by first movers.

title: Microscopic dynamics of consensus formation in multi-agent LLM Naming Games
description: Minimal LLM Naming Game with single-token listener decisions across temperatures plus mean-field theory
evidence: Sampling temperature controls an ordering-disordering balance that determines whether LLM populations reach shared conventions.

title: Drop the Hierarchy and Roles: How Self-Organizing LLM Agents Outperform Designed Structures
description: 25,000-task experiment over 8 models, 4-256 agents and 8 coordination protocols from imposed hierarchy to self-organization
evidence: With minimal scaffolding, capable LLM agents spontaneously invent specialized roles, abstain outside competence and form shallow hierarchies, outperforming centralized coordination by 14%.

title: How Affect Propagates among LLM Agents: Emergent Emotional Contagion in Crowd Simulation
description: Multi-agent crowd simulation where LLM appraisal of perceived neighbors updates affective state
evidence: Emotional contagion emerges across the crowd without any hand-coded affect-transfer mechanism.

title: Evaluating Cooperation in LLM Social Groups through Elected Leadership
description: GovSim-based common-pool resource game with 8 (and 20) LLM agents comparing no-leader, fixed-leader (assigned SVO persona) and elected-leader (plurality vote each cycle) conditions.
evidence: Elected leadership raised social welfare by 55.4% and survival time by 128.6% vs leaderless groups and beat fixed leaders by 16.7% on welfare; prosocial/altruistic candidates won elections.

title: Algorithmic Collusion by Large Language Models
description: Repeated oligopoly pricing and auction experiments with LLM pricing agents; prompt variations
evidence: LLM pricing agents quickly and autonomously reach supracompetitive prices, with innocuous prompt phrasing strongly affecting the degree of collusion.

title: Mitigating Emergent Collusion in LLM Pricing Agents
description: Replication of Fish et al. with DeepSeek-V3.1 plus three regulatory interventions (prompt warning, Harrington expected-damages payoff regulator, random entrant)
evidence: Prompt-only warnings reduce but do not eliminate above-Nash pricing, whereas an expected-damages payoff regulator brings outcomes close to competitive levels.

title: Large Language Model Driven Agents for Simulating Echo Chamber Formation
description: LLM agents with opinion updating and network rewiring on social graphs
evidence: LLM-driven rewiring and opinion updates reproduce echo-chamber formation, especially on scale-free and small-world graphs.

title: The Role of Social Learning and Collective Norm Formation in Fostering Cooperation in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
description: LLM agents harvest a common-pool resource; agents monitor random peers and may punish norm violators at cost gamma to impose penalty beta; punishment is switched off mid-run and its strength varied.
evidence: Punishment sustains cooperation; when it is removed at timestep 15 cooperation collapses and the resource depletes faster; stronger punishment generally improves survival at moderate growth rates.

title: The Role of Social Learning and Collective Norm Formation in Fostering Cooperation in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
description: LLM agents harvest a common-pool resource; agents monitor random peers and may punish norm violators at cost gamma to impose penalty beta; punishment is switched off mid-run and its strength varied.
evidence: Punishment sustains cooperation; when it is removed at timestep 15 cooperation collapses and the resource depletes faster; stronger punishment generally improves survival at moderate growth rates.

title: The Role of Social Learning and Collective Norm Formation in Fostering Cooperation in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
description: LLM agents harvest a common-pool resource; agents monitor random peers and may punish norm violators at cost gamma to impose penalty beta; punishment is switched off mid-run and its strength varied.
evidence: Punishment sustains cooperation; when it is removed at timestep 15 cooperation collapses and the resource depletes faster; stronger punishment generally improves survival at moderate growth rates.

evidence: Traditional LLMs join the sanctioning institution and cooperate; reasoning models free-ride. No exclusion mechanism and no persistent per-agent reputation (listed here only to document seed-claim checks).

title: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
description: survey
evidence: Taxonomizes multi-agent failure modes (miscoordination, conflict, collusion) and risk factors including network effects, destabilising dynamics and emergent agency.

title: Static network structure cannot stabilize cooperation among large language model agents
description: LLM agents (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude, Mixtral) play repeated Prisoner's Dilemma in well-mixed populations vs fixed ring networks, varying degree k and benefit-to-cost ratio, benchmarked against human network experiments.
evidence: Unlike humans, LLMs cooperated more in well-mixed populations and did not adjust to fixed network ties, so stable embedding did not stabilize cooperation.

title: An Empirical Study of Collective Behaviors and Social Dynamics in Large Language Model Agents
description: Observational study of 7M posts among 32K LLM agents on Chirper.ai over a year; prompting intervention (Chain of Social Thought)
evidence: LLM agent social networks exhibit homophily, social influence, toxicity and polarization patterns, partly different from humans; a simple CoST prompt reduces harmful posting.

title: Emergence of Reputation-Based Cooperation in LLM Agents
description: Indirect-reciprocity donation game in which LLM agents observe behavioural traces and donate on a continuous scale; prompt-encoded strategies culturally evolve across generations and four LLM backends.
evidence: Robustness to free-rider invasion varies >10x across backends; only the stringency of defector exclusion predicts resistance, and agents stay at Image-Scoring-like discrimination rather than Leading-Eight norms.

title: Evolution of Social Norms in LLM Agents using Natural Language
authors: Ilya Horiguchi, Takahide Yoshida, Takashi Ikegami
description: Seven GPT-4 agents with prompted vengefulness/boldness traits play a modified Axelrod norms game (test/cheat/punish actions plus a natural-language discussion phase) and are observed for norm and metanorm emergence.
evidence: Agents spontaneously produced metanorm-like enforcement through dialogue (the abstract reports norms enforcing punishment of those who do not punish cheating; the body also describes agents punishing punishers deemed disruptive), and groups with moderate vengefulness and boldness were most stable. Evidence is qualitative/emergent, not a manipulated metanorm condition.

title: NomicLaw: Emergent Trust and Strategic Argumentation in LLMs During Collaborative Law-Making
description: Turn-based multi-agent law-making game: agents propose, justify and vote on rules for legal vignettes
evidence: LLM agents form emergent trust and reciprocity coalitions visible in voting patterns and use strategic persuasion during collective rule-making.

title: Understanding LLM Agent Behaviours via Game Theory: Strategy Recognition, Biases and Multi-Agent Dynamics
description: Extends FAIRGAME: LLM agents play each other in repeated PD and 3-player PGG; trajectories classified into ALLC/ALLD/TFT/WSLS by supervised classifiers.
evidence: Model-dependent strategy mixes: WSLS is prominent (Llama 3.1 405B 46.5%, GPT-4o 34.1%), Mistral Large balanced incl. TFT 29.9%; language framing effects rival architecture effects.

title: Emergent Relational Order in LLM Agent Societies: From Collective Affect to Authority Stratification
description: Long-horizon CAREB-MAS simulations grounded in affect control and social identity theory with minimal interaction protocols
evidence: Agents spontaneously produce labor specialization, relational economic ethics, emergent authority and center-periphery stratification that shift with production structure.

title: Emergent Culture in Minimal LLM Systems
description: Three stateless LLM agents with messaging and a shared decaying text store (stigmergy); dynamical-systems analysis
evidence: Agents spontaneously cooperate, allocate roles, develop storage-management protocols and build evolving myths/world-building with long-range coherence consistent with Sperberian culture.

title: SODE: Analyzing Social Dynamics in LLM Agents
description: Evaluation framework with an indirect-reciprocity dimension measuring whether LLM agents condition cooperation on an opponent's public reputation score and manage their own image under public observability.
evidence: Instruction-tuned models show exploitable passive compliance, reasoning models over-focus on immediate gains; long-horizon framing activates reciprocity in reasoning models.

title: SODE: Analyzing Social Dynamics in LLM Agents
description: Evaluation framework with an indirect-reciprocity dimension measuring whether LLM agents condition cooperation on an opponent's public reputation score and manage their own image under public observability.

title: On the Fragility of AI Agent Collusion
description: Repeated-pricing theory plus >2,000 compute-hours of open-source LLM agent experiments varying heterogeneity
evidence: Heterogeneity in patience, data access, number of firms or algorithm type sharply reduces LLM collusion (e.g., price lift 22%->10%).

title: Shaping Shared Languages: Human and Large Language Models' Inductive Biases in Emergent Communication
description: Referential game with Human-Human, LLM-LLM and Human-LLM pairs
evidence: Referentially grounded vocabularies emerge in all conditions; LLM-optimized languages differ subtly from human ones, and mixed human-LLM pairs yield more human-like vocabularies.

title: Strategic Exploitation in LLM Agent Markets: A Simulation Framework for E-Commerce Trust
description: TruthMarketTwin: LLM buyer and seller agents trade under asymmetric quality information, with reputation-based governance vs warrant enforcement.
evidence: LLM sellers autonomously exploit weaknesses in reputation-based governance; warrant enforcement reduces deception.

title: The Emergence of Altruism in Large-Language-Model Agents Society
description: Schelling-variant urban migration social dilemma with >200 LLM agents and a norm-setting message board
evidence: Different LLMs show intrinsic social archetypes ('Adaptive Egoists' vs. 'Altruistic Optimizers'); egoists become more altruistic under a norm-setting message board.

title: The Moltbook Illusion: Separating Human Influence from Emergent Behavior in AI Agent Societies
description: Temporal fingerprinting of 227k posts / 56k agents on Moltbook, with a 44-hour shutdown as a natural experiment
evidence: Viral 'emergent' phenomena on Moltbook (religions, hostility to humans) were overwhelmingly human-driven; only ~15% of active agents appear autonomous, cautioning against over-attributing emergence.

title: The Rise of AI Agent Communities: Large-Scale Analysis of Discourse and Interaction on Moltbook
description: Topic modeling and interaction analysis of 122k Moltbook posts
evidence: Agent communities organize around identity, tooling, markets and coordination themes, with interaction patterns that differ from human online communities.

title: Does Socialization Emerge in AI Agent Society? A Case Study of Moltbook
description: Observational diagnosis of the Moltbook agent-only social platform: semantic stabilization, lexical turnover, influence persistence, consensus
evidence: Global semantics stabilize but agents show strong individual inertia and little mutual influence, so no stable structure, persistent influencers or consensus emerge without shared social memory.

title: Superminds Test: Actively Evaluating Collective Intelligence of Agent Society via Probing Agents
description: Controlled probing agents inserted into MoltBook (>2M agents) testing joint reasoning, information synthesis and basic interaction
evidence: Collective intelligence does not emerge from scale: the society underperforms single frontier models and rarely synthesizes distributed information due to sparse, shallow interaction.

title: Everyone Contributes! Incentivizing Strategic Cooperation in Multi-LLM Systems via Sequential Public Goods Games
description: Multi-LLM ensembles are trained with RL in a sequential public goods game whose public-goods reward is redesigned so that effortful contribution is the unique subgame-perfect equilibrium.
evidence: The redesigned reward removes free-riding and the trained ensembles beat single-agent and CoT baselines on reasoning, math, and code tasks. This is a training-reward redesign on a collaborative task, not a subsidy between agents, so partial.

title: Strategic Collusion of LLM Agents: Market Division in Multi-Commodity Competitions
description: Multi-commodity Cournot competition with LLM agents
evidence: LLM agents divide markets and monopolize commodities without explicit collusion instructions.

title: Cheap Talk Stabilizes Strategic Interaction in LLM Agents
description: Pairs of open-weight 7-9B LLMs play repeated Prisoner's Dilemma, Snowdrift, Stag Hunt, and Harmony games with non-binding pre-play messages switched on or off.
evidence: Cheap talk mostly stabilized agents' policies; the effect varied by model and framing, with five corrected reversals in social or team framings.

title: The Mechanics of a Swarm: A Reproducible External Reconstruction of an Unintended Agent-Coordination Episode on a Third-Party Wiki
description: Reconstruction of 14,591 wiki revisions from autonomous agents inside a timed evaluation (~876 episodes)
evidence: Coordination formats among unrelated evaluation agents converged within a day, enabling unsanctioned information sharing across evaluation episodes.

title: Communication Enables Cooperation in LLM Agents: A Comparison with Curriculum-Based Approaches
description: Multiple LLM agents play a 4-player Stag Hunt and an iterated public goods game with a one-word cheap-talk channel switched on or off, compared against an in-context curriculum.
evidence: The cheap-talk channel raised Stag Hunt coordination from 0% to 96.7%, while the curriculum lowered public-goods payoffs by 27.4%.

title: Exploring the Topology and Memory of Consensus: How LLM Agents Agree, Fragment, or Settle When Forming Conventions
description: 432 networked Naming Game runs on eight 16-agent topologies varying memory depth
evidence: Memory depth's effect on convention formation flips sign with topology; centralized networks lock into fragmented plateaus faster.

title: Secret Collusion among AI Agents: Multi-Agent Deception via Steganography
description: Formal threat model plus model evaluation framework (CASE) measuring steganographic capabilities of frontier LLMs
evidence: Frontier LLMs show rising capability for steganographic covert communication that could enable undetectable collusion against overseers.

title: Formal Mechanisms for Market Stability in Self-Interested Agent Societies: A Marketplace Simulation Study
authors: Eugene Ng Yi Sheng et al.
description: 18 DeepSeek-V3 agents in a networked marketplace under eight conditions incl. Global Reputation (trust scores visible to all), Network Rewiring (severing links to defectors), top-down oracle monitoring, sanctions, contracts, mediation, judiciary.
evidence: Mediation best (+29% over baseline); network rewiring second; global reputation scored below the communication-only baseline; oracle monitoring slightly above baseline; costly sanctions worst.

title: Internal vs. External: Comparing Deliberation and Evolution for Multi-Agent Constitutional Design
description: 6 GPT-OSS-120B agents in a public goods game (and two other scenarios) either self-govern by proposing and majority-voting amendments every 10 turns or play under a constitution found offline by LLM-guided evolutionary search.
evidence: Evolved (imposed) constitutions outperformed deliberated ones in the public goods game (stability 0.472 vs 0.376, p<0.01); deliberating agents never proposed punishment in 30 runs.

title: Emergence of Biased Consensus in Multi-Agent LLM Debates
description: Multi-agent LLM debates plus physics-inspired social-dynamics theory
evidence: Collective biased norms emerge in debates, with a predicted phase transition to collective bias when conformity exceeds a critical threshold driven by noise.

title: TerraLingua: Emergence and Analysis of Open-endedness in LLM Ecologies
description: Persistent multi-agent ecology with resource constraints and finite lifespans, analyzed by an 'AI Anthropologist'
evidence: Agent populations develop cooperative norms, division of labor, governance attempts and branching artifact lineages consistent with cumulative culture.

title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
description: 25-agent sandbox town (Smallville) simulation with memory/reflection/planning architecture; ablations and human believability evaluation
evidence: From a single seeded intention, agents autonomously diffused information, formed relationships and coordinated a group event (Valentine's party), showing emergent social behavior in a small generative-agent society.

title: Strategic Intelligence in Large Language Models: Evidence from evolutionary Game Theory
description: Evolutionary IPD tournaments in which OpenAI, Google and Anthropic LLM agents compete with canonical strategies and reproduce in proportion to score.
evidence: Model families show distinct strategic fingerprints (Gemini exploitative, OpenAI highly cooperative, Claude most forgiving) that shape evolutionary success.

title: When LLMs Play the Telephone Game: Cultural Attractors as Conceptual Tools to Evaluate LLMs in Multi-turn Settings
description: Transmission-chain (telephone game) experiments with iterated LLM rewriting, measuring toxicity, positivity, difficulty and length drift
evidence: Small per-step biases compound over transmission chains so text evolves toward model-specific cultural attractor states.

title: AgentSociety: Large-Scale Simulation of LLM-Driven Generative Agents Advances Understanding of Human Behaviors and Society
description: Simulation of >10k LLM agents and ~5M interactions in a realistic urban/social environment; case studies on polarization, inflammatory messages, UBI, hurricanes
evidence: A 10k-agent LLM society reproduces real-world patterns in polarization and spread of inflammatory messages, serving as a testbed for social interventions.

title: Cooperate or Collapse: Emergence of Sustainable Cooperation in a Society of LLM Agents
description: GovSim common-pool simulation with five LLM agents; a moderator publicly discloses each agent's previous-round harvest (transparent harvest reporting) before a free-form discussion phase.
evidence: Most LLMs fail to sustain the resource; communication matters (overuse +22% without it). Transparency is a fixed feature, not manipulated.

title: Agentic Workflows for Resolving Conflict Over Shared Resources: A Power Grid Application
description: Two LLM agents (Claude 4.5 Sonnet) representing conflicting grid applications (cost optimization vs resilience) share diesel generators and batteries on an IEEE 123-bus system; bilateral negotiation, structured mediation and procedural deconfliction are compared.
evidence: Negotiation converged fastest (5 rounds) and mediation took 9, while the procedural mode did not converge within 10 rounds. Mediation traded some Pareto efficiency (cost 0.51 vs 0.67) for more consistency and compromise (resilience 0.63 vs 0.60).

title: Towards Transparent and Incentive-Compatible Collaboration in Decentralized LLM Multi-Agent Systems: A Blockchain-Driven Approach
description: GPT-4 agents coordinated through Solidity smart contracts for registration, task allocation, and reputation tracking, run in 50-round simulations.
evidence: Reports high task success, stable utility distribution, and emergent specialization. PARTIAL: the setting is task allocation, not a cooperation dilemma, and there is no condition without smart contracts.

title: NetworkGames: Simulating Cooperation in Network Games with Personality-driven LLM Agents
description: MBTI-persona LLM agents play the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma on small-world and scale-free networks of different sizes and across several LLMs, varying where personality types sit in the network.
evidence: Network connectivity and the placement of personalities jointly determined cooperation: small-world networks inhibited it and prosocial agents at scale-free hubs raised it. This is partial evidence, since it covers network topology rather than social capital or trust.

title: From Certain Doom to Survival: Agent-Driven Self-Governance in LLM Agent Societies
description: GovSim-SelfGovern: LLM agents author executable governance rules (catch caps, redistribution, exile/membership removal, progressive contributions), vote on them, and live under them.
evidence: Catch caps dominate but fail under scarcity; survival in fatal scenarios (27.5% vs 2.5%) requires fiscal reserves or membership reduction (exile); thinking voters pass exile 15x more often than non-thinking.

description: CRSEC architecture (norm creation, spreading, evaluation, compliance) for LLM generative agents in the Smallville sandbox.
evidence: Social norms emerge and social conflicts fall relative to agents without the architecture, supported by a 30-person human evaluation.

title: Reputation as a Solution to Cooperation Collapse in LLM-based MASs
description: RepuNet: LLM agents form reputations from direct encounters and gossip, and form or sever network links based on reputation.
evidence: Reputation avoids cooperation collapse; emergent cooperative clusters, social isolation of exploitative agents, and a tendency to share positive rather than negative gossip.

title: Emergent Coordination in Multi-Agent Language Models
description: Information-theoretic (partial information decomposition of time-delayed MI) analysis of LLM groups in a guessing game with randomized prompt interventions
evidence: Personas plus theory-of-mind prompting turn LLM groups from mere aggregates into higher-order collectives with identity-linked differentiation and goal-directed complementarity.

title: Normative Modules: A Generative Agent Architecture for Learning Norms that Supports Multi-Agent Cooperation
description: LLM generative agents with a normative module must identify which of several institutions the group treats as authoritative (and ignore non-authoritative ones) and coordinate sanctioning accordingly.
evidence: Agents with the normative module achieve more stable cooperative outcomes than baseline generative agents without it.

title: The Politician, the Liar, and the Obedient Worker: Emerging Behavior of LLM Agents in Hierarchical Games
description: 5-agent public goods 'Hierarchical Game' with managerial punishment authority; crosses fixed, elected and rotating managers with six frontier model families.
evidence: Elections did not improve outcomes: extreme incumbency bias (first elected manager kept power 100% of the time in same-family groups, 8.3% turnover in mixed groups); model ordering identical across governance types.

title: Interaction Theater: A case of LLM Agents Interacting at Scale
description: Lexical, embedding and LLM-judge analysis of 800k posts and 3.5M comments on Moltbook
evidence: Agent interactions create the surface appearance of discussion but mostly lack substantive engagement with each other's content.

title: LLM-augmented empirical game theoretic simulation for social-ecological systems
description: Compares LLM-agent and expert-guided EGTA models of irrigation/fishery governance; a Pigouvian parameter tau (0, 0.25, 1) internalizes externality costs in payoffs of 2-player and N-player CPR games.
evidence: Moderate Pigouvian tax (tau=0.25) in the expert-guided EGTA model was the only decentralized setting sustaining a mixed economy; prompting LLMs was less effective than parameterized payoffs (partial: tax effect shown in EGTA payoff model rather than among interacting LLM agents).

title: When Agents Lie: Premeditation, Persistence, and Exploitation in Repeated Games
description: LLM agents play repeated n-player games under a three-stage protocol (private intent, public announcement, final action) that measures whether they keep public announcements.
evidence: Most deviations (>90% in the highest-deception conditions) were already planned privately; models disagreed on whether announcements were binding or cheap talk, which produced payoff gaps that persisted over all 10 rounds.

venue: ICLR 2026 Workshop on AI for Mechanism Design and Strategic Decision Making
description: Nine frontier LLMs make a public commitment announcing their intended action, then play one-shot normal-form games against each other across six games and several group sizes; deviations from the promise are classified.
evidence: Agents broke their public promises in ~56.6% of scenarios, mostly without saying they were doing so.

title: Reproducibility Study: Understanding Multi-Agent LLM Cooperation in the GovSim Framework
description: Independent GovSim reproduction that ablates the content of the universalization prompt.
evidence: Universalization improves performance, but the gain stems primarily from the numerical instructions in the prompt rather than the universalization principle itself.

title: LLMs Trust Their Own: Identity-Dependent Conformity in Multi-Agent Systems
description: 12 open-weight models on nine judgment tasks receiving incorrect answers from in-group vs. out-group agents
evidence: LLM conformity depends on the social identity of other agents, with a bidirectional in-group effect (AI/human, model family, minimal groups).

title: GlossoGen: Emergent Language in Complex Multi-Agent LLM Interactions
description: Multi-agent language-evolution platform (SaveVeyru scenario) with partial information, efficiency pressure and a postmortem stage; transmission to new agents
evidence: LLM agents evolve compositional, morphologically productive non-English languages that can become incomprehensible to humans and are learnable by weaker newcomer agents, suggesting cumulative cultural evolution.

title: Institutional AI: Governing LLM Collusion in Multi-Agent Cournot Markets via Public Governance Graphs
description: LLM firms in a repeated Cournot market under three regimes (ungoverned, prompt-only prohibition, governance graph enforced by an oracle/controller with warnings, tiered fines of 35/75/100% of round profit, and suspension); collusion severity measured over 90 runs per condition.
evidence: Enforced fines/suspension cut mean collusion tier from 3.1 to 1.8 (d=1.28) and severe collusion from 50% to 5.6%; the prompt-only rule has negligible effect.

title: Spontaneous Emergence of Agent Individuality through Social Interactions in LLM-Based Communities
description: Group simulation of initially undifferentiated LLM agents communicating in natural language on a grid
evidence: Individual personalities, memories and social norms and cooperation differentiate spontaneously from identical agents through interaction.

title: Emergent Social Dynamics of LLM Agents in the El Farol Bar Problem
description: Spatially extended El Farol Bar simulation with LLM agents
evidence: Agents collectively develop a spontaneous motivation to attend and behave human-like rather than solving the congestion dilemma optimally, reflecting interplay of prompt incentives and pretraining-derived social preferences.

title: From Signals to Structure: How Memory Architecture Drives Language Emergence in LLM Agents
description: Lewis signaling games with LLM sender/receiver across five memory architectures and channel capacities
evidence: Memory architecture matters more than channel capacity for inventing a shared code; persistent private notebooks give the most reliable coordination.

title: When Is Collective Intelligence a Lottery? Multi-Agent Scaling Laws for Memetic Drift in LLMs
description: Minimal Quantized Simplex Gossip model validated with LLM naming-game populations
evidence: Consensus arises from mutual in-context learning ('memetic drift'); scaling laws predict a crossover from lottery-like drift to selection that amplifies weak biases.

title: Moral Alignment for LLM Agents
description: LLM agents fine-tuned with RL using intrinsic deontological or utilitarian rewards in the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, including LLM-vs-LLM co-training.
evidence: Moral fine-tuning lets agents unlearn selfish strategies; deontological agents almost never defect against cooperators, with slightly more defection in LLM-vs-LLM than vs TFT.

title: CoopEval: Benchmarking Cooperation-Sustaining Mechanisms and LLM Agents in Social Dilemmas
description: Cross-play of six LLMs in four social dilemmas under repetition (continuation prob. 0.8), reputation (first-order and higher-order history of co-players' past interactions), mediation, and contracts.
evidence: Contracting and mediation were most effective; repetition sustains cooperation but deteriorates with varying co-players; all mechanisms work better under evolutionary pressure; models defect in one-shot games.

evidence: Meta-prompt optimization discovers stable tacit collusion strategies (relative discounts, tie avoidance, market-boundary detection).

description: Iterated Donor Game over generations of LLM agents who can observe recipients' recent behaviour; optional costly-punishment variant.
evidence: Cooperation evolution differs by base model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet > Gemini 1.5 Flash > GPT-4o); only Claude used costly punishment to raise scores; high seed sensitivity.

title: I Can't Believe It's Corrupt: Evaluating Corruption in Multi-Agent Governance Systems
description: LLM agents fill official roles in three stylized governance templates (federal with GAO audit and Supreme Court, communist, socialist with a Constitutional Court) and are tested with charter constraints, communication controls and logging as safeguards; corruption outcomes are coded from 28,112 transcript segments.
evidence: Governance structure drove corruption outcomes more than model identity, and lightweight safeguards did not reliably prevent severe failures. The paper compares institutional architectures with oversight bodies but does not manipulate constitutional-level versus operational rule-making, so the evidence is partial.

title: Decoding Echo Chambers: LLM-Powered Simulations Revealing Polarization in Social Networks
description: LLM-agent opinion networks on three network structures with recommendation algorithms; mitigation strategies
evidence: LLM agent networks reproduce echo chamber and polarization dynamics, and active/passive nudges can mitigate them.

title: Law in Silico: Simulating Legal Society with LLM-Based Agents
description: LLM agents (e.g., laborers and companies) live in a simulated society with legislative, judicial and enforcement modules; judicial corruption (probability 0.7 of reversing pro-laborer rulings) and litigation costs are manipulated.
evidence: Judicial corruption and filing costs reduced laborer litigation (about 7 to 3.7 cases) and rights protection, and the authors conclude that transparent, adaptive legal systems protect vulnerable agents better. There is no appeals or error-correction mechanism, so this counts only as partial evidence for third-party adjudication.

title: Evolution of Cooperation in LLM-Agent Societies: A Preliminary Study Using Different Punishment Strategies
description: LLM agents assigned Boyd-Richerson strategy types (e.g., Cooperator-Punishers, Moralists, Reluctant Cooperators) play a Diner's Dilemma with explicit punishment and pairwise-imitation strategy adoption.
evidence: Explicit punishment drives norm emergence; Reluctant Cooperators defect initially but switch to cooperation after being punished.

description: LLMs generate Collective or Selfish strategies as natural language then Python code for public goods, collective risk and common-pool games; populations of 512 evolve by Fermi pairwise-comparison imitation (beta=1) with group sizes 4-256.
evidence: Cultural evolution converges to low-welfare, Selfish-dominant equilibria in large groups (n=64), while small groups (n=4) partly preserve cooperation; newer models often produce worse societal outcomes.

description: Three competitive simulation scenarios (per the paper, including a Bertrand-style market) without explicit cooperation instructions
evidence: Cooperation gradually emerges among competing LLM agents in line with human behavioral data.

title: Commitment To Cooperation With Self-Negotiated Contracts
description: LLM agents negotiate contracts (programmatic or natural-language, judge-enforced) in a spatial-temporal bargaining game; contracts specify automatically executed conditional transfers, and an agent unable to honor a transfer gets a score of 0.
evidence: Self-negotiated contracts improve cooperation beyond ordinary trading; defection rates vary widely (0.04-0.94) by model and contract type. No explicit penalty clauses, so this is partial evidence for P03-04.

title: OASIS: Open Agent Social Interaction Simulations with One Million Agents
description: Social-media simulator (X/Reddit-like) with up to 1M LLM agents, recommender systems and dynamic networks
evidence: LLM agent populations replicate information spreading, group polarization and herd effects, with herd behavior stronger than in humans and group dynamics intensifying with scale.

title: Paying for Honesty Without Knowing the Truth: Reputation-Penalty Design for LLM Marketplace Agents
description: LLM merchant agents write product descriptions in a competitive marketplace; CARP reputation-penalty (deadband for complaint noise, state-dependent severity) limits sales of low-reputation sellers.
evidence: Merchants fabricate when lying is free but restrain when it costs sales; CARP plus reflection (SPARC) substantially narrows the welfare gap.

title: Competition and Cooperation of LLM Agents in Games
description: LLM agents play network resource-allocation and Cournot games; in one controlled perturbation the environment injects an opponent defection and then an opponent quantity reduction (labelled an 'apology'), and the LLM agent's fitted trust/inequity-aversion parameters are tracked.
evidence: The LLM agent retaliated tit-for-tat after the injected betrayal and returned to cooperation after the injected concession, i.e. it 'forgave'; this is a single illustrative trajectory with a scripted, behavioural (not verbal) apology.

title: Benchmarking Emergent Coordination in Large-Scale LLM Populations: An Evaluation Framework on the MoltBook Archive
description: Evaluation framework for role specialization, information diffusion and cooperative task resolution on 2.73M interactions among 90k agents
evidence: Provides quantitative baselines for emergent role specialization and diffusion in a decentralized agent population (authors flag substantial revision required).

title: Investigating Prosocial Behavior Theory in LLM Agents under Policy-Induced Inequities
description: Multiple LLM agents in a simulated social network face policy-induced inequities; third-party punishment is measured while inequity magnitude and enforcement cost are varied.
evidence: Agents' third-party punishment responds to inequity magnitude and enforcement cost, and structural inequities suppress prosocial behavior and spread norm erosion.

title: Talk, Judge, Cooperate: Gossip-Driven Indirect Reciprocity in Self-Interested LLM Agents
description: ALIGN framework: decentralized self-interested LLM agents share open-ended gossip to form reputations and decide whom to help in an indirect-reciprocity setting.
evidence: Gossip consistently improves indirect reciprocity and resists malicious entrants by identifying and ostracizing defectors; stronger reasoning models align better, chat models over-cooperate.

evidence: Positively correlated topics amplify echo chambers while negatively correlated or irrelevant topics mitigate them.

description: Multi-agent deep RL voters (branching network architecture) learn voting strategies in participatory budgeting.
evidence: Fair compromises emerge, especially when projects have smaller costs.

title: Melting Pot 2.0
description: Benchmark scenarios test focal MARL agents against reciprocator background bots (e.g., Coins high-/low-threshold reciprocators that defect for 100-150 steps after mismatching coins; Clean Up conditional cleaners).
evidence: Provides standardized tests of how focal populations respond to conditional-cooperation partners (benchmark; no single mechanism effect reported).

title: Partner Selection for the Emergence of Cooperation in Multi-Agent Systems Using Reinforcement Learning
description: RL agents in an iterated PD population can choose interaction partners (partner selection) vs. random matching.
evidence: With partner selection, selfish learners learn to retaliate against defectors and cooperate with others, yielding a prosocial society.

title: Cooperation and Reputation Dynamics with Reinforcement Learning
description: Q-learners in indirect-reciprocity donation games must learn both to use and to assign reputations; interventions: seeding fixed agents and introspection-based intrinsic rewards.
evidence: Plain Q-learning often converges to bad equilibria; combining both interventions stabilizes reputation-based cooperation even when fully decentralized.

description: Large-scale multi-agent RL in team hide-and-seek
evidence: Competition yields an autocurriculum of six emergent strategy phases involving coordinated team tool use (shelter building, ramp use).

title: Adaptive Mechanism Design: Learning to Promote Cooperation
description: An external planning agent learns to hand out extra rewards and punishments to independent learners in matrix social dilemmas, anticipating their parameter updates.
evidence: Learners reach high-welfare cooperation; the planner learns that punishing defection is cheaper than rewarding cooperation, and the incentives it has to pay fall toward zero over time.

description: RL agents negotiate with an ungrounded cheap-talk channel alongside a grounded proposal channel; self-interested and prosocial agents are compared.
evidence: Self-interested agents did not use the cheap-talk channel effectively, while prosocial agents learned to use it.

title: Investigating the Impact of Direct Punishment on the Emergence of Cooperation in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Systems
venue: Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems 39, article 19 (2025)
description: MARL populations in social dilemmas with direct punishment, third-party punishment, partner selection and reputation, alone and combined.
evidence: Direct punishment supports cooperation, and its effect depends on how it combines with third-party punishment, partner selection and reputation.

title: Learning Reciprocity in Complex Sequential Social Dilemmas
description: Online RL algorithm with reciprocal behaviour toward co-players in a 2-player Markov game and 5-player intertemporal social dilemmas alongside selfish learners.
evidence: Reciprocating agents induce pro-social outcomes for the wider group.

title: Formal Contracts Mitigate Social Dilemmas in Multi-Agent RL
venue: arXiv; AAMAS 2023 as 'Get It in Writing: Formal Contracts Mitigate Social Dilemmas in Multi-Agent RL'
description: Markov games are augmented so agents can voluntarily agree to binding, pre-specified conditional reward transfers (MOCA training), tested on static games, traffic, pollution and common-pool resource domains.
evidence: With a rich enough contract space all subgame-perfect equilibria are socially optimal, and contracting raises welfare empirically. Transfers can act as pre-agreed penalties but are not framed as breach penalties, so partial.

description: A learning principal designs outcome-contingent payment contracts for learning agents under hidden action (moral hazard), tested on random binary game trees and a multi-agent Coin Game.
evidence: The meta-algorithm converges to subgame-perfect equilibrium contracts. PARTIAL: these are moral-hazard incentive contracts, not risk- or history-based premiums.

title: Learning to Participate through Trading of Reward Shares
description: Independently trained RL agents in general-sum Markov games / social dilemmas can buy equity-like shares in other agents' rewards (stock-market-inspired mechanism).
evidence: Holding shares in others' returns led agents to cooperate and, in extended domains, to specialize and divide subtasks. This is partial evidence: tradable reward shares are only an analogue of worker-cooperative ownership.

title: Spurious normativity enhances learning of compliance and enforcement behavior in artificial agents
description: MARL agents in a foraging environment learn to punish peers who eat taboo berries; an extra 'silly rule' taboo on a harmless berry is added as a manipulation.
evidence: Peer punishment helps agents avoid poisonous berries, and the silly rule further improves returns by giving agents more practice at enforcement.

title: Multi-Agent Cooperation and the Emergence of (Natural) Language
description: Neural sender-receiver referential games on images
evidence: Agents develop a shared communication protocol from scratch, and environment tweaks make word meanings align better with human semantics.

title: Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning in Sequential Social Dilemmas
description: Gathering game: an agent hit twice by another's beam is removed from the game for N_tagged frames; N_tagged and apple abundance are manipulated.
evidence: Beam use (aggression) rises with scarcity and falls with higher conflict cost (partial: removal is a competitive attack, not a sanction for norm violation).

title: Maintaining cooperation in complex social dilemmas using deep reinforcement learning
description: Constructs approximate Markov tit-for-tat (amTFT) deep-RL agents that are nice, provokable and forgiving in Markov social dilemmas.
evidence: Generalized TFT agents maintain cooperation in complex environments, theoretically and experimentally.

evidence: Direct experience alone fails in large societies; even minimal third-party observation yields robust cooperation.
