description: Independent RL agents in a shared environment with experts; tests whether agents learn to imitate/learn from others, with a model-based auxiliary loss.
evidence: Vanilla model-free agents do not use social learning, but with environment constraints and auxiliary loss they learn from experts and outperform solo-trained agents.

title: Learning and Sustaining Shared Normative Systems via Bayesian Rule Induction in Markov Games
description: Agents assume a shared normative system and infer norms by Bayesian rule induction from others' compliance and sanctions in Markov games (resource management, labour compensation).
evidence: Newcomers rapidly adopt established norms and groups converge on shared norms that sustain cooperative institutions, with far less experience than model-free norm learning.

title: AI-Enhanced Distributed Channel Access for Collision Avoidance in Future Wi-Fi 8
description: Wi-Fi stations are trained with constrained MAPPO (centralized training, decentralized execution) to choose channel-access and backoff behavior, compared against standard binary exponential backoff (BEB) in dense deployments.
evidence: The learned access policy cut collision probability relative to BEB and removed starvation under a fairness metric. This benchmarks MARL against exponential back-off on a shared channel; it is not framed as a social dilemma.

title: A multi-agent reinforcement learning model of common-pool resource appropriation
description: Independent deep RL agents in a partially observed common-pool resource Markov game (with a tag-out beam)
evidence: Emergent exclusion and territoriality arise among independent learners, linking exclusion, sustainability and inequality.

title: A memory-based spatial evolutionary game with the dynamic interaction between learners and profiteers
description: Spatial evolutionary game where 'profiteers' imitate highest-payoff neighbours via the Fermi rule and 'learners' use Q-learning, with Markov role switching and payoff memory.
evidence: Interaction between Fermi imitators and Q-learners fosters cooperation; memory helps profiteers cooperate and higher learning rates increase cooperators.

title: Bottom-Up Reputation Promotes Cooperation with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
description: LR2: agents learn a cooperation policy and a reputation-assignment policy from local observations in spatial social dilemmas, without predefined norms.
evidence: Bottom-up reputation assignment reshapes rewards and produces strategy clustering that sustains cooperation.

title: Bottom-Up Reputation Promotes Cooperation with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
description: LR2: agents learn a cooperation policy and a reputation-assignment policy from local observations in spatial social dilemmas, without predefined norms.
evidence: Bottom-up reputation assignment reshapes rewards and produces strategy clustering that sustains cooperation.

title: Truthful and Trustworthy IoT AI Agents via Immediate-Penalty Enforcement under Approximate VCG Mechanisms
venue: IEEE Internet of Things Journal (2026, per arXiv)
description: Multi-agent RL bidders trade energy in an approximate-VCG double auction with a one-shot penalty for misreporting; allocation accuracy and penalty level are varied.
evidence: Learned agents converged to truthful reporting near the theoretically predicted penalty threshold, and better allocation accuracy reduced incentives to deviate.

title: The Role of Network Topology and Opponent Information in Shaping Cooperation in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Systems
description: Deep RL agents placed as nodes of graphs play iterated Prisoner's Dilemma with neighbours; network topology and the opponent information available (action history, identity) are manipulated.
evidence: Neighbours per node and average path length were the main drivers of emergent cooperation; opponent identity information reduced cooperative strategy adoption.

title: Learning to cooperate with emergent reputation via multi-agent reinforcement learning
description: COOPER jointly learns reputation assessment rules and reputation-based policies from environment rewards on social networks.
evidence: Adapts to existing reputation systems and co-players; reputation norms and cooperation co-emerge in self-play, robust across network topologies.

title: Learning to cooperate with emergent reputation via multi-agent reinforcement learning
description: COOPER jointly learns reputation assessment rules and reputation-based policies from environment rewards on social networks.
evidence: Adapts to existing reputation systems and co-players; reputation norms and cooperation co-emerge in self-play, robust across network topologies.

title: Adaptive Punishment for Cooperation in Mixed-Motive Games
description: APC: learned defection-awareness module sets punishment probability and severity according to detected defection in sequential social dilemmas.
evidence: Reduces costly, ineffective punishment and outperforms baselines (partial for P08-02: conditions punishment intensity on defection but never switches to reward).

title: Adaptive Punishment for Cooperation in Mixed-Motive Games
description: APC: learned defection-awareness module sets punishment probability and severity according to detected defection in sequential social dilemmas.
evidence: Reduces costly, ineffective punishment and outperforms baselines (partial for P08-02: conditions punishment intensity on defection but never switches to reward).

title: Adaptive Punishment for Cooperation in Mixed-Motive Games
description: APC: learned defection-awareness module sets punishment probability and severity according to detected defection in sequential social dilemmas.
evidence: Reduces costly, ineffective punishment and outperforms baselines (partial for P08-02: conditions punishment intensity on defection but never switches to reward).

title: Modeling Moral Choices in Social Dilemmas with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
description: RL agents with intrinsic rewards encoding different moral frameworks (consequentialist vs norm-based) interact in Prisoner's Dilemma, Volunteer's Dilemma and Stag Hunt.
evidence: Different internalised moral reward types produce different patterns of cooperation, defection and exploitation among agents.

title: Deconstructing Cooperation and Ostracism via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
description: Two RL agents play repeated PD, each with a cooperation policy and a network-rewiring (connect/disconnect) policy.
evidence: Rewiring facilitates cooperation via learned ostracism of defectors, but ostracism emerges from and then reinforces cooperation rather than causing it alone.

title: A learning agent that acquires social norms from public sanctions in decentralized multi-agent settings
description: Decentralized RL agents see all public sanctioning events; the architecture includes a classifier of approved/disapproved behavior and a motivation to punish in step with the group.
evidence: Agents acquire beneficial sanctioning norms that reduce free-riding and raise per-agent returns.

title: A learning agent that acquires social norms from public sanctions in decentralized multi-agent settings
description: Decentralized RL agents see all public sanctioning events; the architecture includes a classifier of approved/disapproved behavior and a motivation to punish in step with the group.
evidence: Agents acquire beneficial sanctioning norms that reduce free-riding and raise per-agent returns.

title: A learning agent that acquires social norms from public sanctions in decentralized multi-agent settings
description: Decentralized RL agents see all public sanctioning events; the architecture includes a classifier of approved/disapproved behavior and a motivation to punish in step with the group.
evidence: Agents acquire beneficial sanctioning norms that reduce free-riding and raise per-agent returns.

title: Evolving intrinsic motivations for altruistic behavior
description: Deep RL agents in intertemporal social dilemmas with a modular architecture whose intrinsic-reward module evolves under multi-level (group) selection.
evidence: Evolved intrinsic motivations produce cooperative inductive biases, learned model-free.

title: Emergent Prosociality in Multi-Agent Games Through Gifting
description: Self-interested learning agents in multi-equilibrium (high-risk coordination) games may transfer part of their reward to peers; analysed with dynamical-systems theory and simulations.
evidence: Gifting enlarged the basins of attraction of prosocial equilibria and substantially improved convergence to them without external reward shaping.
code: voluntary transfer of reward to peers

title: Resolving social dilemmas with minimal reward transfer
description: Defines a 'general self-interest level' and computes minimal reward-transfer structures that make the social optimum dominant in multi-player social dilemmas.
evidence: Minimal reward redistribution can align individual and group incentives; the work is mostly analytical, so partial.

title: Learning to Incentivize Other Learning Agents
description: Each RL agent learns an incentive function to give rewards directly to other agents, accounting for its effect on their learning, in social dilemmas (e.g., Escape Room, Cleanup).
evidence: Learned peer incentives beat standard RL and often reach a near-optimal division of labor. This is peer-to-peer reward, not a central subsidy.

title: The AI Economist: Taxation policy design via two-level deep multiagent reinforcement learning
description: A planner learns tax schedules with redistribution while a population of RL economic agents co-adapts (two-level deep RL).
evidence: Learned tax policies improve the equality-productivity trade-off over baselines despite tax-gaming. The setting is an economy rather than a social dilemma, so partial for P04-02.

title: Evolution of cooperation in the public goods game with Q-learning
description: Spatial public goods game on a lattice with Q-learning agents, compared against the Fermi imitation-rule baseline, with and without voluntary participation.
evidence: Cooperation emerges more readily under Q-learning than under Fermi imitation; voluntary participation produces a non-monotonic dependence of cooperation.
code: option to opt out of game

title: Learning to Negotiate via Voluntary Commitment
description: Markov Commitment Games in which RL agents may voluntarily commit to proposed future plans, with a commitment protocol learned by policy gradient plus incentive-compatible learning.
evidence: Converged faster and reached higher returns than baseline methods in mixed-motive tasks.

title: Learning to Negotiate via Voluntary Commitment
description: Markov Commitment Games in which RL agents may voluntarily commit to proposed future plans, with a commitment protocol learned by policy gradient plus incentive-compatible learning.
evidence: Converged faster and reached higher returns than baseline methods in mixed-motive tasks.

title: Gossip & reputation spreading
description: In tight-knit communities, word spreads fast about who isn't pulling their weight. A 2012 study found gossip about free-riders travels faster than direct observation — and deters cheating effectively.
evidence: Feinberg et al. (2012) Psychological Science; Nowak & Sigmund (2005) Nature (indirect reciprocity / image scoring)

title: Reputation score / credit system
description: Your Uber driver rating, eBay seller feedback, or social credit score — a running number that unlocks or restricts access based on track record. Drop below a threshold and you lose privileges automatically.
evidence: Dellarocas (2003) Management Science; Uber/eBay ratings; China social credit

title: Cryptographic audit log / immutable transparency
description: A permanent, tamper-proof record — every action logged and attributable forever. Not a punishment itself, but makes punishment possible by guaranteeing detection. Sanction-enabler: you can't enforce norms you can't see.
evidence: Nakamoto (2008) Bitcoin whitepaper; Kolt (2024) Governing AI Agents; Pierucci et al. (2026) governance graphs

title: Ostracism, exile & social shunning
description: Temporary or permanent exclusion — from a village, a platform, or a trade network. Lab experiments show even the threat of expulsion nearly doubles cooperation in public goods games.
evidence: Cinyabuguma et al. (2005) J. Public Econ.; Gürerk et al. (2006) Science

title: Suspension of access / licence revocation
description: Temporarily losing access to the shared resource — your fishing licence suspended for a season, or locked out of an irrigation channel. Time-limited exclusion that signals seriousness without being permanent.
evidence: Baland & Platteau (1996) Halting Degradation; Ostrom (1990) graduated sanctions

title: Allowlist / denylist
description: Email spam filters (Spamhaus blocklist) — once flagged, no one receives your messages. Binary, automatic exclusion with no gradation. Fast and scalable but can catch legitimate senders in friendly fire.
evidence: Ramachandran & Feamster (2006) SIGCOMM; email spam filters (Spamhaus)

title: Ridicule, shaming & social disapproval
description: The low-level embarrassment of showing up empty-handed to a potluck, or being the only one not contributing to a group gift. Subtle but powerful in close-knit groups — stigma is a cost even without formal rules.
evidence: Masclet et al. (2003) AER (non-monetary punishment); Feinberg et al. (2012)

title: Altruistic punishment (Fehr-Gächter)
description: Humans will spend their own money to punish a stranger who cheated — even in a one-shot game where they'll never meet again. Fehr & Gächter proved this experimentally. Anger at unfairness, not self-interest, drives it.
evidence: Fehr & Gächter (2002) Nature; Guzman, Jin et al. (2025) SanctSim

title: Fixed fine / traffic fine / auto-penalty
description: A speed camera issues a fine automatically the moment you exceed the limit. No discretion, no negotiation — fast and cheap to administer. Automatic triggering means no cost of detection beyond the technology.
evidence: Mookherjee & Png (1994) JPE; Ostrom (1990)

title: Pre-agreed contractual penalty (liquidated damages, penalty clause)
description: A pre-agreed penalty for breach — like a builder who owes £500/day for every late day, agreed before work starts. Avoids court arguments about 'what harm did this actually cause?' by fixing the cost upfront.
evidence: Cavendish Square v. Makdessi [2015] UKSC 67; Beale et al. (2019) Ius Commune

title: Proof-of-stake slashing
description: Ethereum validators lock up their own money ('stake') before they can participate. If they cheat — e.g. signing two conflicting blocks — the protocol automatically destroys part of that stake. Real skin in the game.
evidence: Ethereum PoS spec; Saleh (2021) RFS; EigenLayer restaking (correlated slash)

title: Sentencing guidelines (standardised formula)
description: Standardised formula for deciding punishments — like US Federal Sentencing Guidelines — so similar crimes get similar sentences regardless of the judge. Reduces arbitrariness and improves perceived fairness.
evidence: US Sentencing Commission (2023) Guidelines Manual

title: Token toxicity (self-defeating attack cost)
description: To attack the Ethereum network you'd need to buy 51% of all staked ETH — but buying that much drives up the price, and attacking the network destroys its value. The attacker defeats themselves. Self-defeating defection.
evidence: Buterin (2014) Ethereum Whitepaper

title: Restaking & correlated slash
description: EigenLayer lets the same Ethereum stake secure multiple systems at once. If any of those systems detects misbehaviour, all stakes across all systems can be cut simultaneously — amplifying punishment for coordinated attacks.

title: Praise, status elevation & prestige
description: Generous people get celebrated — hunters who share meat gain status; potlatch hosts earn community prestige. Henrich & Gil-White show prestige is a distinct human status mechanism that rewards contribution.
evidence: Henrich & Gil-White (2001) Evolution & Human Behavior; Guzman, Jin et al. (2025) SanctSim

title: Pigouvian subsidy / grant for public good
description: Government grants for solar panels pay you to do something socially good. Lab research found subsidies can be more efficient than fines in public goods contexts — especially when cooperation is already widespread.
evidence: Andreoni et al. (2003) AER (carrot or stick); Guzman, Jin et al. (2025) SanctSim

title: Staking reward / validator yield
description: Honest Ethereum validators earn around 3–5% annual yield on their staked ETH — paid automatically for doing their job correctly. The reward makes the threat of slashing credible: you have something real to lose.
evidence: Saleh (2021) RFS; Roughgarden (2021) ACM EC

title: Nudge & default-setting
description: UK auto-enrolment pensions (2012): instead of asking people to opt into savings, they're enrolled automatically and must actively opt out. Participation jumped from ~60% to 90%+ overnight — without any new incentive.
evidence: Thaler & Sunstein (2008) Nudge; UK auto-enrolment pensions

title: Carrot/stick choice (Andreoni)
description: A manager choosing between praising high performers vs. docking pay for low ones. Both work. Context matters: punishment edges reward in most lab settings, but reward is more effective when cooperation is already high.

title: Peer reward / gifting
description: Group members pay a cost to transfer a reward to peers who contributed (reward treatment of lab public-goods games).
evidence: Andreoni et al. (2003) AER; Sefton, Shupp & Walker (2007) Economic Inquiry

title: Ostrom graduated sanctions (warning → fine → suspension)
description: The 'yellow card' — a formal notice before any real penalty. Ostrom's research on Swiss alpine meadows and Spanish irrigation systems showed that jumping straight to fines makes people resentful and abandon the commons.
evidence: Ostrom (1990) Governing the Commons; Swiss alpine meadows, Spanish irrigation

title: Graduated throttling / QoS degradation
description: Mobile data slowing from full speed to 2G after you've used your monthly allowance — still usable, but degraded. Graduated response proportional to how far over the limit you've gone. No hard cutoff.
evidence: RFC 1633 (integrated services); mobile data throttling

title: Exponential back-off
description: After a failed login, wait 1 second. After another failure, 2 seconds. Then 4, 8, 16... An automated escalating delay that makes brute-force attacks cost-prohibitive without blocking legitimate users permanently.
evidence: Karn & Partridge (1987) SIGCOMM; TCP congestion control

title: Governance graph (state machine: Warning→Suspended→Fined→Active)
description: A compliance state machine: new employee → trained → certified → flagged → suspended → reinstated. Each state has defined rules and transitions enforced at runtime. Applied to AI agents by Pierucci et al. (2026).
evidence: Pierucci et al. (2026) governance graphs (preprint)

title: Cheap talk / public pledge (non-binding)
description: Non-binding pre-game pledges, UN declarations, or simply saying 'let's all be fair' before starting. Surprisingly effective: even cheap promises shift behaviour by creating shared expectations everyone can point to.
evidence: Sally (1995) Rationality & Society; Cialdini (1984) Influence; Piatti, Jin et al. (2024) GovSim

title: Binding commitment device (costly to reverse)
description: A savings club where you hand your money to a treasurer who won't return it until year-end. Or a pre-committed gym contract. Removes temptation by making it costly to back out — Odysseus tied to the mast.
evidence: Ashraf et al. (2006) QJE (Tying Odysseus to the mast)

title: Deposit / reputation bond
description: A tenant's security deposit — paid upfront, returned if you behave. Construction performance bonds work similarly. The money at stake makes your commitment credible before you've done anything.
evidence: Klein & Leffler (1981) JPE; tenant security deposits, construction bonds

title: Smart contract auto-execution
description: A smart contract that releases payment to a builder automatically when a sensor confirms the building is complete — no lawyers, no court, no negotiation. The code runs itself the moment conditions are met.
evidence: Szabo (1997) First Monday; Ethereum smart contracts

title: Resource taboo / sacred no-take zone
description: Traditional 'no-take' zones enforced by cultural taboo — certain days, certain waters, certain forests. Scientists have found these informal rules often outperform formal regulations in protecting shared resources.
evidence: Cinner & Aswani (2007) Biological Conservation; traditional MPAs
code: restrict use in zones or seasons

title: Voluntary public commitment
description: Making a public pledge is much harder to break than a private one. Paris Agreement signatories, fundraising challenges, and pre-commitment apps all use this. Cialdini's 'commitment & consistency' principle.

title: Hard rate limit (API/bandwidth)
description: When an app sends too many requests per second, the server simply stops responding — a hard ceiling. Prevents one user from hogging a shared resource and starving everyone else. Standard in cloud computing (AWS, Google Cloud).

title: Collective punishment (all penalised for one defection)
description: If one player cheats, everyone shares part of the penalty — creating strong internal pressure to self-police. Airline crew are collectively penalised if security is breached, so they monitor each other.
evidence: Olson (1965) Logic of Collective Action; Abbink et al. (2017) Nature Comms

title: Cross-default / solidarity lending
description: A credit union where one member's default raises borrowing costs for everyone — creating strong social pressure to stay current. HOA fees and solidarity lending groups (Grameen Bank) use the same mechanism.
evidence: Besley & Coate (1995) J Dev Econ; Grameen Bank; HOA fees

title: Mutual aid pooling / decentralized bail fund
description: A community bail fund pools small donations to post bail for any arrested member — no credit check, no bureaucracy. Grameen Bank solidarity groups work similarly: the group covers anyone who can't repay, creating mutual accountability.
evidence: Yunus (1999) Banker to the Poor; Feigenberg et al. (2013) REStud

title: Tit-for-Tat / Win-Stay Lose-Shift
description: I'll cooperate as long as you do.' Tit-for-Tat won Axelrod's famous computer tournament against hundreds of strategies. Win-Stay Lose-Shift refines it to avoid endless retaliation. The simplest conditional strategy outperforms complex ones.
evidence: Axelrod (1984) Evolution of Cooperation; Akata et al. (2025); FAIRGAME (2025)

title: Threshold-based reward/punish switch
description: A fishing cooperative that gives bonuses when stocks are healthy (cooperation is high) but switches to fines when stocks dip below a threshold (cooperation is low). Adapts the sanction tool to current conditions automatically.
evidence: Andreoni et al. (2003) AER; Zhang et al. (2025) Research Policy

title: Pigouvian tax (externality pricing)
description: A carbon tax charges companies per tonne of CO₂ emitted, making pollution expensive and nudging toward cleaner choices. Named after economist Arthur Pigou (1920). Sweden's carbon tax (over $130/tonne) is the world's highest.
evidence: Pigou (1920) Economics of Welfare; Nordhaus (2007); Sweden carbon tax

title: Reputational indirect reciprocity
description: You help a stranger not because they helped you, but because others can see you helping and will trust you more later. Nowak & Sigmund call this 'image scoring' — cooperation maintained by reputation, not direct exchange.

title: Elected monitor / legitimate authority
description: A democratically elected compliance officer gets far better cooperation than one appointed top-down. A field experiment in Uganda found elected monitors improved contribution rates significantly vs. randomly assigned ones.
evidence: Baldassarri & Grossman (2011) PNAS; Uganda field experiment

title: Participatory budgeting
description: Porto Alegre (Brazil) from 1989 let citizens vote on how to spend part of the city budget — residents prioritised their actual neighbourhood needs. Now used in hundreds of cities worldwide. Contribution to deliberation = influence.
evidence: Wampler (2007) Penn State UP; Porto Alegre (Brazil) 1989+

title: DAO token voting & veto
description: MakerDAO token holders vote on interest rates and risk parameters for its stablecoin. Token holders with bigger stakes have more votes. Democratic in theory, but large holders can dominate — a known flaw.
evidence: MakerDAO governance; Buterin (2014); Mehar et al. (2019)

title: Institutional self-selection (choose your regime)
description: People voluntarily choosing to live under stricter rules because they trust the institution. A Science paper by Gürerk et al. (2006) showed lab participants migrated toward sanctioning institutions — even from a free-rider paradise.
evidence: Gürerk et al. (2006) Science; Guzman, Jin et al. (2025) SanctSim

title: Whistleblower leniency / cartel immunity
description: The first cartel member to confess to antitrust authorities gets immunity from prosecution. Creates a 'race to confess' that breaks up cartels faster than any external investigation could. EU leniency programme has broken up hundreds of cartels.
evidence: EU Leniency Programme; race to confess in antitrust

title: Apology & confession as norm repair
description: Corporate public apologies after scandals; Japanese corporate bowing ceremonies; Catholic confession as norm-repair ritual. Research shows a sincere apology reduces retaliatory impulse in victims even when no material compensation follows.
evidence: Tavuchis (1991) Mea Culpa; Lazare (2004) On Apology

title: Truth & reconciliation (amnesty for disclosure)
description: South Africa's Truth & Reconciliation Commission offered amnesty in exchange for full public disclosure of crimes committed under apartheid. The act of honest truth-telling was itself part of the repair — not just a condition for leniency.
evidence: South Africa TRC; Tutu (1999); Hayner (2011) Unspeakable Truths

title: Material repair & restitution (restore actual harm)
description: A vandal required to repaint the wall they damaged — physical restoration of actual harm, not just a fine paid into a central fund. Restorative justice research shows repair assignments reduce re-offending more than equivalent fines.
evidence: Braithwaite (1989) Crime, Shame and Reintegration; Zehr (2015) Little Book of Restorative Justice

title: Rehabilitation programme (structured re-entry)
description: The path back in after being suspended — conditional re-entry, parole with requirements, community reintegration programmes. Ostrom's design principles explicitly include this: the goal is restoration, not permanent exile.
evidence: Ostrom (1990) design principles; drug courts; Travis (2005) But They All Come Back

title: Community reconciliation
description: Rwanda's gacaca courts and Northern Ireland's community dialogue processes both focused on rebuilding the relationship between offender and community — not just punishing the offender. Victims reported higher satisfaction than with conventional courts.
evidence: Rwanda gacaca courts; Clark (2010) Cambridge UP

title: Metanorm: punish non-punishers
description: The social expectation to call out someone who lets rule-breaking slide ('you saw what he did and said nothing?'). Axelrod showed this 'metanorm' can stabilise enforcement systems that would otherwise unravel.
evidence: Axelrod (1986) APSR
code: sanction those who fail to sanction

title: Anti-social punishment filter
description: "In some cultures, people punish those who cooperate too much — 'tall poppy syndrome,' spite, or resentment. Herrmann et al. (2008) found this antisocial punishment in lab experiments across 16 countries. A filter prevents it from corrupting the system.
evidence: Herrmann et al. (2008) Science (anti-social punishment across 16 countries)

title: Constitutional vs. operational rules (nested tiers)
description: "A country's constitution vs. its everyday laws. Constitutional rules are harder to change and govern how other rules are made. Ostrom's design principle 8: stable commons governance needs these nested tiers — who decides who decides.
evidence: Ostrom (1990) Ch. 6; Kelsen (1945) General Theory of Law and State

title: Formal appeals & contestability
description: The right to appeal a parking fine, a sacking, or an algorithmic decision — a formal check against arbitrary sanctions. GDPR Article 22 gives EU citizens the right to contest automated decisions that affect them.
evidence: GDPR Art. 22; Mashaw (1983) Bureaucratic Justice

title: Mediation & arbitration
description: Resolving disputes through an independent third party rather than courts — faster, cheaper, and private. The ICC handles thousands of international commercial arbitrations per year. Ostrom's design principle 6 emphasises accessible conflict resolution.
evidence: ICC International Court of Arbitration; Ostrom design principle 6

title: False-positive correction
description: A system for fixing mistakes — wrongful convictions overturned, fraud flags cleared, automated bans reversed. The Innocence Project has exonerated 200+ US prisoners through DNA evidence. Critical in AI systems that will misclassify.
evidence: Innocence Project; GDPR Art. 22

title: Code-is-law vs. hard fork (social override)
description: In 2016 a hacker legally drained $60M from a smart contract by exploiting its code. The Ethereum community voted to rewrite history and reverse the transaction — overriding 'code is law' via a community hard fork.
evidence: 2016 DAO hack & Ethereum hard fork; DuPont (2017) Routledge

title: Universalization prompting ('what if everyone did this?')
description: The 'what if everyone did that?' question — used by parents, teachers, and Kant's ethics alike. A 2024 AI governance study found prompting AI agents with this question improved sustainable resource choices significantly.
evidence: Piatti, Jin et al. (2024) GovSim; Kant's categorical imperative

title: Fermi imitation (copy successful neighbours)
description: Watching what your most successful colleagues do and copying their approach. Cultural evolution works the same way — we learn by imitating those who seem to be doing well. Strategy spreads through a population without central planning.
evidence: Boyd & Richerson (1985) Culture and the Evolutionary Process

title: Algorithm generation (Willis-style tournaments)
description: High-frequency trading algorithms compete in financial markets — each algorithm is a strategy, and markets evolve by selecting which survive. Applied to cooperation games by Willis & Mourant to study how sanctioning strategies evolve.
evidence: Axelrod (1987) genetic algorithms; Warnakulasuriya et al. (2024)

title: VCG mechanism (truthful dominant strategy)
description: A special auction design (used by Google for ad slots) where telling the truth about your valuation is always your best move — the mechanism is designed so honesty dominates every other strategy. No policing needed.
evidence: Vickrey (1961); Clarke (1971); Groves (1973); Google ad auctions

title: Token-curated registry (stake to challenge entries)
description: A decentralized list of 'trusted' sources — anyone can challenge an entry by staking tokens. If your challenge is upheld, you earn; if it fails, you lose your stake. Crowd-sourced quality control with real financial incentives.
evidence: de la Rouviere (2017) TCR 1.0

title: Moral hazard premium
description: Drivers with a history of speeding pay higher car insurance — the premium internalises the extra risk they impose on everyone else. Deductibles work similarly: you bear part of any loss, making you more careful.

title: Timebanking & community currency
description: A local timebank where 1 hour of babysitting earns 1 time credit — redeemable for 1 hour of someone fixing your bike. Every hour of any task is equal. Used widely in COVID-19 mutual aid networks across the UK and US.
evidence: Cahn (2000) No More Throw-Away People; LETS systems; Mondragon

title: Generalised reciprocity / gift economy
description: Open-source software — you contribute code, someone else benefits, someone else contributes back, with no direct exchange. Wikipedia works the same way. Kropotkin argued this gift-economy logic was the original human economy.
evidence: Kropotkin (1902) Mutual Aid; Benkler (2006) Wealth of Networks; open-source software

title: Network embeddedness / social capital (Putnam)
description: Why do regions with lots of civic clubs (choirs, sports leagues, neighbourhood associations) end up with better-functioning governments and less corruption? Putnam's landmark Italian study: dense social networks build generalised trust.
evidence: Putnam (1993) Making Democracy Work; Baldassarri (2015) AJS

title: Worker cooperative (ownership as incentive alignment)
description: At Mondragon every worker owns part of the cooperative and gets one vote regardless of seniority. Profits are shared. Incentives align because everyone's success depends on collective effort — ownership replaces punishment.
evidence: Mondragon; Pencavel (2013) JEEA; Whyte & Whyte (1991)

title: Mesh network / offline resilience
description: Meshtastic devices used in disaster zones (California wildfires, Puerto Rico after Hurricane Maria) keep communications alive when phone towers fail — a peer-to-peer radio mesh that anyone can join and relay.
evidence: Meshtastic; Vega et al. (2012) IEEE; Puerto Rico post-Maria

title: Solidarity & mutual accountability
description: A mutual aid group where members check in on each other, call each other out gently when something is wrong, and share responsibility — no boss, no formal rules. Horizontal accountability between equals.

title: Blockchain-based mutual aid DAO
description: Gitcoin's quadratic funding gives proportionally more weight to many small donors than to one large donor — making it harder for wealthy actors to dominate community funding decisions. Anti-plutocratic by design.
